question.text: Which SEBI regulation governs the exit load on ELSS (Equity Linked Savings Schemes) mutual funds?

answer.text: ELSS schemes cannot charge any exit load because of the mandatory 3-year lock-in period
ELSS schemes can charge a maximum exit load of 1% if redeemed within 5 years
ELSS schemes can charge exit load only during the first year at a rate of 2%
ELSS schemes must charge a mandatory exit load of 0.50% on all redemptions

explanation.text: The Logic: Equity Linked Savings Schemes (ELSS) are equity-oriented mutual fund schemes eligible for tax deduction under Section 80C of the Income-tax Act and carry a mandatory three-year lock-in from the date of each investment. Because units cannot be redeemed during the lock-in period, there is no occasion to charge an exit load on those units — once the three-year lock-in is over, units can be redeemed without any exit load. In practice, ELSS schemes therefore do not levy an exit load. The Trap: A 1% exit load if redeemed within 5 years, a 2% exit load in the first year, and a mandatory 0.50% exit load on all redemptions all imply that ELSS units could be redeemed within the lock-in or that an exit load is structurally needed — both of which contradict the way ELSS is designed. The three-year lock-in itself functions as the commitment device, replacing the need for an exit load. Note: The cited pages of the NISM Series V-A Mutual Fund Distributors workbook (p.161-p.162, p.165) confirm ELSS Section 80C eligibility and the three-year lock-in, but the specific statement that ELSS schemes cannot charge any exit load on account of the lock-in was not located in the pages checked. The framing above is general ELSS product-design knowledge. The stem references "regulation" loosely; the underlying fact (no exit load on ELSS units) is a product-design consequence of the mandated lock-in.
